text:
Enterprise Architecture spent 30 years trying to create stable target-state systems.

AI just changed the rules.

Now, value streams can rip out pieces of Oracle, Workday, SAP, or Salesforce and replace them with vibe-coded AI-native systems in weeks instead of years.

At first, it looks like innovation.

Then the enterprise starts turning into a Jenga tower:
* local optimization everywhere
* structural integrity nowhere
* hidden dependencies multiplying underneath the surface

The real danger is not AI replacing architects.

It is enterprises fragmenting themselves faster than organizational coherence can survive.

The old North Star was a destination.

The new North Star is a survivability model for continuous architectural mutation.

That changes Enterprise Architecture forever.

How do we grow architects when AI is dismantling the very career path that used to produce them?

That question landed on a whiteboard a few weeks ago, during a working session with a colleague on the upskilling path towards the architect role. What are the ultimate skills we still need to deliberately train?

I could not let it go. So I spent several days pulling the thread: passionate discussions with colleagues, and a few rather animated debates with Claude and Gemini, both of whom remained suspiciously enthusiastic about a future that still needs human architects!

Where I landed: the answer may have been sitting on our bookshelves for years. From Christopher Alexander to the Gang of Four to cloud native to today's agentic patterns, there is a lineage, and underneath it, a grammar that has not moved while every technology around it changed.

The article makes the case: six invariant forces, one genuine mutation brought by agentic AI, and what it all means for how we should train the next generation of end-to-end architects.

But it is an intuition under construction, published to be stress-tested. Is your architect pipeline breaking the way ours is? Does your list of invariants match mine? I genuinely want to compare notes.

author_headline: Successful, future-oriented office workplaces and meeting cultures for a hybrid, digital reality - where physical presence is intentional and value is measurable.
text:
Most Organisations Are Running a Twenty-First-Century Business on a Twentieth-Century Operating System.

Knowledge work is changing faster than most organisations are capable of adapting. Artificial intelligence, digital technologies, new employee expectations, and increasingly distributed ways of working are fundamentally reshaping how value is created. Yet many organisations continue to manage work through structures, leadership models, and governance systems designed for a different era - one where work was location-dependent, information was scarce, and coordination relied on physical proximity.

The result is a growing mismatch between how work actually happens and how organisations are designed to support it.

Today, knowledge work is increasingly digital, distributed, and AI-mediated. Workflows span functions, locations, technologies, and increasingly humans and machines. Yet responsibility for the workplace, technology, people, and organisational performance often remains fragmented across separate departments and leadership domains.

Many organisations are therefore attempting to govern a twenty-first-century work system with a twentieth-century operating model.

This may become one of the defining competitive challenges of the coming decade. The organisations that succeed will not simply adopt new technologies. They will redesign the organisational operating systems through which knowledge work is coordinated, governed, and enabled.

The AI coding revolution is eating you alive, and you don't even see the trap.

You think the problem is quality. It's not. It's volume.

Humans review code at O(n). AI generates at exponential speed. You become a cyborg—not enhanced, but reduced to a biological lint-roller, drowning in output you cannot verify, performing a theater of diligence while your actual craft withers.

Here's the paradox: the more you cling to reading every line, the more obsolete you become.

The escape? Stop writing code. Start writing laws. 

Sovereign Architects don't instruct machines—they define universes where invalid solutions cannot exist. They build "Compound Reliability" through orthogonal verification channels. They become god-like: not building everything, but deciding what can exist at all.

This is software development's industrial revolution: from craft to systematic discipline. From verification clerk to lawgiver.

The choice is binary: Cyborg nightmare or Architect ascension.

The trap is already snapping shut. Read this before you lose your soul.

author_headline: Only 27% of AEC firms are actually using AI in their day-to-day operations today.
text:
Only 27% of AEC firms are actually using AI in their day-to-day operations today.

But the overwhelming majority say they're about to pour serious investment into it over the next few years.

Sit with that gap for a second. Because that gap is not a footnote — it's the entire story of what's about to happen to architecture education.

Walk into most architecture schools right now and the curriculum still looks eerily familiar to what existed 20 years ago: hand sketching, design theory, a semester of AutoCAD, maybe a rushed crash course in Revit somewhere in the final year, taught almost like an afterthought.

Now walk onto an actual construction site. Projects are being delivered through digital twins. Clash detection happens before a single beam is fabricated. Cost and schedule are simulated in 4D and 5D before ground is even broken. 

Sustainability isn't a chapter in a textbook anymore — it's a compliance requirement baked into every single design decision from day one.

The gap between what's taught and what's practiced isn't just wide. It's quietly deciding who gets hired and who doesn't, five years from now.

So we sat down and asked a harder question than "what software should students learn."

We asked: what kind of thinking will the built environment actually demand by 2030 — and what does a classroom built for THAT future actually look like?

The answer isn't more software modules bolted onto an unchanged curriculum. It's a complete mindset shift — from architect as sole author of a drawing, to architect as orchestrator of an intelligent, data-rich building lifecycle.

In our latest newsletter, we break down the six capabilities we believe will actually define the architect of 2030:

→ Information fluency — reading a carbon report as fluently as a floor plan 
→ Full lifecycle systems thinking — designing for year 10 performance, not just handover day 
→ AI-augmented design with retained human judgment — knowing WHY an AI-generated option is wrong, not just accepting the fastest one
→ Coordination as design quality, not admin overhead 
→ Sustainability as a day-one input variable, not a late-stage checkbox 
→ Fluency in open standards and Common Data Environments

None of this is about chasing software trends. It's the same transformation medicine went through with data-driven diagnostics, or finance went through with quantitative modelling — the core skill is shifting from craft-as-execution to craft-as-informed-judgment.

At the Forrester CX East conference in June, I shared some thoughts on the future of the CX/VoC profession and how first-party customer feedback will be even more important in the AI era.

Enterprise AI systems can ingest CRM data, call transcripts, product usage, support tickets, and countless other signals. But those signals are often incomplete, inferred, or biased.

Clozd customer data has already shown that:
- 85% of loss reason fields in the CRM are wrong
- 77% of decision drivers in won or lost deals never surface in call recordings
- 65% of competitor fields in the CRM are wrong

This is why companies will need continuous feedback loops that bring first-party customer reality into their AI stack - to confirm, expand, correct, and contradict what AI thinks it knows.

And that changes the future of VoC.

I believe the best VoC leaders will evolve from running feedback programs to becoming architects of the Truth Layer - keeping the entire enterprise AI stack grounded in the customer.

text:
Not every instructional designer should use AI the same way.

A junior ID and a mid-level ID may both be working on a storyboard, but they are not bringing the same level of judgment, pattern recognition, or design confidence to the task.

So why should AI support them in exactly the same way?

For junior IDs, AI should act more like a mentor — explaining, guiding, modeling better practice, and helping them build the foundations of instructional design.

For mid-level IDs, AI should act more like a collaborator and critic — challenging assumptions, pressure-testing assessments, comparing design options, and sharpening judgment.

The real opportunity is not just faster course creation.
It is maturity-sensitive AI use that helps IDs grow at the right level.

This article explores how junior and mid-level instructional designers can use AI differently — without turning it into a crutch.

I’m excited to share a project I’ve been working on: **SecondSelf AI**, a RAG-based AI assistant designed to turn personal documents and knowledge into an interactive AI system.

Instead of manually searching through multiple documents, SecondSelf AI allows you to ask questions in natural language and get answers based on the information contained in your knowledge base.

For example:
🔹 “What projects have I worked on?”
🔹 “What are my technical skills?”
🔹 “Summarize my experience.”
🔹 “What information is available about this topic?”

The system uses **Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)** to:
→ Process and understand document-based knowledge
→ Retrieve relevant information for a user's question
→ Provide the relevant context to the AI
→ Generate a meaningful, context-aware response

author_headline: Agentic AI Solutions in Energy & Automation I CRA consulting
text:
🎇 我最近問了幾位設備商的朋友同一個問題。
你的傳送模組供應商，是在賣一支手臂給你，還是在跟你一起設計子系統？
多數人愣了一下，因為這兩件事在採購系統裡長得一模一樣，都是一個料號、一個單價、一個交期。
但它們的差別，會在你開發下一代機台的時候現形。
賣手臂的，等你把規格定完再報價。跟你一起設計的，在你還在畫架構圖的時候就坐在會議室裡。前者是成本項，後者是開發資源。
這個差別，正好也解釋了為什麼全球晶圓傳送機器人的玩家幾十年下來始終只有十餘家。門檻不在專利，而在別的地方。
我把EFEM產業的生態系分工、領先者的四種打法，以及 AI 正在改變的變數，寫成了這週的電子報。裡面也提到台灣在這份全球名單上的位置，我想很多人會意外。 🦾 

I asked several equipment makers the same question recently.
Is your wafer handling supplier selling you a robot, or designing a subsystem with you?
Most paused. In a procurement system these look identical. One part number, one unit price, one lead time.
The difference shows up when you develop your next platform.
A robot vendor quotes after your specs are frozen. A design partner is in the room while you are still sketching the architecture. One is a cost line. The other is engineering capacity you did not have to hire.
That distinction also explains something odd about this industry. Despite decades of semiconductor growth, the number of credible wafer transfer players has stayed in the low teens. The barrier is not patents. It is something harder to buy.
This week I mapped the full ecosystem, from AMHS and load ports through the EFEM to the process chamber, the four plays that separate the leaders, and what AI is changing on both the demand side and the moat side.
There is also a note on where Taiwan sits on the global supplier list. That part surprised a few people.

AI killed the wireframe. Claude Design just brought it back!

A year ago wireframes joined the long LinkedIn list of things that are dead. Why sketch in grey boxes when you can have a polished, interactive prototype in minutes?
I was one of the people pushing back. At the Scope Conference in the UK, I argued that wireframing still mattered: for research, for design thinking, for stakeholder alignment.
One year later, somewhat ironically, Claude Design launched with a wireframe mode built in. And then it struck me: beyond the design and research arguments, there might be a third reason not to skip wireframes in an AI-assisted workflow. An economic one.

I explored this idea in an article and I am curious whether this resonates. Does that make sense for you? I would love to get your thoughts!

author: Raja Raj
author_headline: CSE Graduate || Graphic Designer || Al & Tech Content Creator || Data Science || Python || Data Analysis/
text:
AI, ML, LLM, GPT… wait, aren’t they all the same thing? 

If AI terminology feels like a never-ending alphabet soup, here’s the easiest way to make sense of it.

Think of it like a ladder 👇

1️⃣ AI — The big umbrella
Artificial Intelligence is the overall idea of making machines perform tasks that require human-like intelligence.

2️⃣ ML — Learning from data
Machine Learning is one way to build AI systems — instead of programming every rule, we let models learn patterns from data.

3️⃣ Neural Networks — Learning through layers
These are ML models inspired by how interconnected neurons process information, making it possible to learn complex patterns.

4️⃣ Deep Learning — More layers, more complexity
Deep Learning uses neural networks with many layers to learn increasingly sophisticated representations.

5️⃣ Transformers — The architecture behind modern AI
Transformers use attention mechanisms to understand relationships between different parts of data. They became the foundation for many modern language and multimodal models.

6️⃣ Generative AI — Creating something new
Instead of only predicting or classifying, Generative AI can create text, images, audio, video, and code.

7️⃣ LLMs — Language-focused models
Large Language Models are trained on massive amounts of text to understand and generate human language.

8️⃣ GPT — A family of Transformer models
GPT stands for Generative Pre-trained Transformer — a family of models built using the Transformer architecture.

9️⃣ ChatGPT — The product you interact with
ChatGPT is a conversational AI product that uses GPT models along with other technologies to provide an interactive experience.

The easiest mental model:

AI → Big umbrella
↓
ML → A way to build AI
↓
Neural Networks → A type of ML model
↓
Deep Learning → Neural networks with many layers
↓
Transformers → A powerful deep-learning architecture
↓
LLMs → Language-focused models
↓
GPT → A Transformer-based model family
↓
ChatGPT → A product built around these technologies

And Generative AI?
Think of it as a capability that can sit across different types of models — generating content rather than simply analysing it.

Once you see the relationship, terms like AI, ML, LLM, GPT and ChatGPT stop sounding like completely different technologies.

Save this for the next time AI terminology gets confusing.

author: Trevor Meeks
author_headline: Partner at Meeks + Partners | Multifamily Design That Performs
text:
Everyone is pointing AI at renderings, and the tools are genuinely good. But rendering was never the bottleneck.

The most useful place we have found for AI so far is construction administration.

Construction administration is a different kind of problem. It is site reports, RFI responses and submittal reviews, and it is relentless. 

A project in the field generates a steady volume of documents that all need reading, cross checking against the drawings, and answering accurately and quickly. Miss something in a submittal review and it shows up as a change order months later.

That is what we are testing against. 

Organizing the material, pulling the relevant sheets and details together, and flagging where a submittal does not match what was drawn.

The gain we are after is accuracy before speed. CA mistakes are expensive, and they are usually failures of attention rather than judgment, which is exactly the kind of work worth handing to a machine.

The other reason construction administration is the right place to start is that the output is checkable. A submittal either matches the drawing or it does not, and you find out inside a day. That is not true of a design suggestion, where being wrong stays invisible until much later.

None of this is finished and some of it will not hold up. 

We are testing it on real work rather than in a demo, which is the only way to find out.

If you have architects on your projects using AI in construction administration already, I would be interested to hear what is actually working.

Bringing Back the YAMA House: AI-Assisted Architectural Visualization

I recently revisited a project from my time at Mojo Stumer Architects (2014)—the YAMA House, designed by the brilliant Peter Johns under the direction of Mark Stumer, for client Mr. Rahinzada.

text:
Everyone is pointing AI at renderings, and the tools are genuinely good. But rendering was never the bottleneck.

The most useful place we have found for AI so far is construction administration.

Construction administration is a different kind of problem. It is site reports, RFI responses and submittal reviews, and it is relentless. 

A project in the field generates a steady volume of documents that all need reading, cross checking against the drawings, and answering accurately and quickly. Miss something in a submittal review and it shows up as a change order months later.

That is what we are testing against. 

Organizing the material, pulling the relevant sheets and details together, and flagging where a submittal does not match what was drawn.

The gain we are after is accuracy before speed. CA mistakes are expensive, and they are usually failures of attention rather than judgment, which is exactly the kind of work worth handing to a machine.

The other reason construction administration is the right place to start is that the output is checkable. A submittal either matches the drawing or it does not, and you find out inside a day. That is not true of a design suggestion, where being wrong stays invisible until much later.

None of this is finished and some of it will not hold up. 

We are testing it on real work rather than in a demo, which is the only way to find out.

If you have architects on your projects using AI in construction administration already, I would be interested to hear what is actually working.

Giving Life to an Architectural Vision.

There is something incredibly fascinating about seeing a design come alive.

You see people occupying the spaces.

AI-generated renderings look stunning in pitch decks, but they quickly turn into a nightmare during the execution phase.

Recently, an international architect came to us with a gorgeous AI-generated interior concept. The client loved the mood, but as soon as feedback came in asking for specific layout adjustments, the "AI trap" sprung:
- Lack of spatial consistency: Prompting AI to re-render the same room with minor tweaks yielded completely different furniture scale, modified lighting, and altered structural boundaries.

- Impractical physics: The AI visual relied on non-standard geometry and custom elements that were impossible to source or construct in reality.

- Wasted billable hours: Instead of making quick revisions, the architect spent endless hours fighting prompts to keep the design consistent—costing time, budget, and credibility.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗦𝗼𝗹𝘂𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻: Our team took the original AI concept and rebuilt the entire scene from scratch using standard 3D modeling and precise BIM workflows.

Now, the client gets the best of both worlds:
1. Exact material accuracy and realistic lighting.
2. Complete parametric flexibility—allowing fast, precise adjustments to furniture, layouts, or lighting without breaking the visual integrity of the space.

AI is fantastic for rapid ideation, but when it’s time to revise, build, and deliver, structured 3D modeling is still irreplaceable.

“Does it look photorealistic?”

“Does it communicate the design?”

Because a client doesn't look at a rendering the way a 3D artist does.
 
They want to understand:
 
→ What will this space feel like?
 → Does the material selection make sense?
 → How will natural light change the atmosphere?
 → Can I imagine myself in this space?
 → Does this help me make a decision?
 
That’s why I believe visualization is not just about creating beautiful images.

It's about turning an idea into something people can understand emotionally and practically.
 
And with AI + 3D modeling + rendering technology evolving so quickly, the opportunity for architects and designers is becoming even bigger.

The technology can create the visual.
 The real skill is knowing what the visual needs to communicate.

author: Rajesh Mane
author_headline: Building AI Agents | Generative AI | Data Science | Artificial Intelligence | Agentic AI | RAG | Making AI accessible
text:
This is one of the most complete breakdowns of Generative AI I’ve seen.

It connects probability, architectures, training, and real systems in one flow.

1] Generative vs discriminative models

• Generative models learn p(x) or p(x, y) 
• Discriminative models learn p(y | x) 

This is the core shift.

Instead of classification → you learn the entire data distribution.

2] Probability + latent space

• Models approximate p_data(x) using pθ(x) 
• Latent variables z simplify complex distributions 
• Generation becomes sampling from learned distributions 

Every model is solving density estimation.

3] Core architectures

• VAE → latent space + ELBO optimization 
• GAN → generator vs discriminator minimax game 
• Diffusion → learn to reverse noise step-by-step 
• Transformers → next-token prediction at scale 

Different methods, same goal: generate realistic data.

4] Training pipeline

• Pretraining → learn general patterns from massive data 
• Fine-tuning → adapt to specific tasks 
• Instruction tuning → follow natural language instructions 
• RLHF → align outputs with human preferences 

Modern LLMs are multi-stage systems, not single models.

5] How generation actually happens

• Autoregressive models → predict token by token 
• Diffusion → start from noise, iteratively denoise 
• GAN → generate and refine via adversarial feedback 

Different generation mechanics → different strengths.

A simple way to think about it:

Traditional ML learns boundaries.

Generative AI learns the full data distribution.

Once you understand this shift, every model architecture starts to make sense.

A practical GenAI project can be thought of as a lifecycle:

→ Identify the use case
Define the problem, users, requirements, and expected outcome.

→ Experiment and select
Evaluate available foundation models and choose one that fits the task.

→ Adapt, align, and augment
Improve the model with techniques such as fine-tuning, alignment, retrieval, and additional data when needed.

→ Evaluate
Measure quality, accuracy, relevance, safety, and other task-specific requirements.

→ Deploy and integrate
Connect the model to the application, infrastructure, data, and workflows.

→ Monitor and improve
Track how the system performs in production and iterate based on what you learn.

And this is where things get interesting.

A production GenAI application isn’t just:

User → LLM → Answer

It can involve:

→ Foundation models
→ Prompting
→ Retrieval and external knowledge
→ Vector databases
→ Tools and APIs
→ Application logic
→ Evaluation
→ Monitoring
→ Security and governance

The model is an important component.

But the surrounding architecture determines how useful that model becomes.

So instead of starting a GenAI project with:

“Which model should we use?”

Start with:

“What problem are we solving, and how will we measure whether it works?”

That shift can completely change how you approach GenAI engineering.

A practical GenAI project can be thought of as a lifecycle:

→ Identify the use case
Define the problem, users, requirements, and expected outcome.

→ Experiment and select
Evaluate available foundation models and choose one that fits the task.

→ Adapt, align, and augment
Improve the model with techniques such as fine-tuning, alignment, retrieval, and additional data when needed.

→ Evaluate
Measure quality, accuracy, relevance, safety, and other task-specific requirements.

→ Deploy and integrate
Connect the model to the application, infrastructure, data, and workflows.

→ Monitor and improve
Track how the system performs in production and iterate based on what you learn.

And this is where things get interesting.

A production GenAI application isn’t just:

User → LLM → Answer

It can involve:

→ Foundation models
→ Prompting
→ Retrieval and external knowledge
→ Vector databases
→ Tools and APIs
→ Application logic
→ Evaluation
→ Monitoring
→ Security and governance

The model is an important component.

But the surrounding architecture determines how useful that model becomes.

So instead of starting a GenAI project with:

“Which model should we use?”

Start with:

“What problem are we solving, and how will we measure whether it works?”

That shift can completely change how you approach GenAI engineering.
